title: Correlation vs causation and confounding
reading_md:
**What it is.** Correlation means two things move together. Causation means changing one changes the other. A confounder drives both: shopping frequency drives both app use and spend, so app users spend more even if the app changes nothing. Ways to separate them:

- randomisation, as in an A/B test;
- comparing within segments of similar customers;
- control groups.

**How to work it out.**

Within-segment difference = metric for group 1 in segment s - metric for group 2 in segment s

Worked example. App users spend €60, other customers €40. Among heavy shoppers, app users spend €80 and others €78. Among light shoppers, €35 and €34.

- Naive gap = 60 - 40 = €20.
- Heavy-shopper gap = €2. Light-shopper gap = €1 (whole euros).
- Most of the €20 comes from who uses the app: heavy shoppers use it more. Within segments the gap is only €1 to €2.

**In the interview.** "Name a confounder for 'stores with more staff sell more'." A model answer: "Store size or footfall. Bigger, busier stores get more staff and also sell more, so staff and sales move together even if extra staff add no sales."

**Common mistakes.**

- Treating a strong correlation as proof of cause.
- Controlling for a variable that the treatment itself changes, which hides part of the effect.
- Assuming no correlation means no causation: two effects can cancel out.
